result:
The correct answer is Solution 1 ($C = 12\pi$), though its supporting claims for other surfaces are only sketched.

For $\mathbb{CP}^2$ with any Kähler class $[\omega]=t h$, the Chern scalar curvature integrates to $\int S\,\omega^2/2 = 2\pi\,c_1\cdot[\omega] = 6\pi t$ over volume $t^2/2$, so $m \le 12\pi/t$. Every nontrivial integral class is a multiple of the line class, and calibration gives $\operatorname{sys}_2 = t$, so $m\cdot\operatorname{sys}_2 \le 12\pi$, with equality for Fubini–Study. This shows $C \ge 12\pi$ outright.

Solution 2 claims $\mathbb{CP}^2$ gives 3, which uses an unjustified normalization ($S=3$ with $\operatorname{sys}_2=1$) and contradicts the computation above.

Solution 3 claims 8π is attained on $S^2\times S^2$, but $\mathbb{CP}^2$ already exceeds 8π, so it cannot be the smallest universal constant.

For the other surfaces I checked, the bounds are smaller than $12\pi$: $S^2\times S^2$ gives at most $8\pi$, and $\mathbb{F}_1$ gives at most $20\pi/3$. I did not verify every case (e.g., ruled surfaces over higher-genus curves or further blowups), so the upper bound $C \le 12\pi$ rests on the pattern across the cases I checked.

CHOICE: 1
CONFIDENCE: 4
